{{Short description|Equations for correlation functions in QFT}}
[[File:Freeman Dyson.jpg|thumb|Freeman Dyson in 2005]]

{{technical|date=May 2025}}The '''Schwinger–Dyson equations''' ('''SDEs''') or '''Dyson–Schwinger equations''', named after [[Julian Schwinger]] and [[Freeman Dyson]], are general relations between [[correlation function (quantum field theory)|correlation functions]] in [[quantum field theory|quantum field theories]] (QFTs). They are also referred to as the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]]s of quantum field theories, since they are the [[Equation of motion|equations of motion]] corresponding to the Green's function. They form a set of infinitely many functional differential equations, all coupled to each other, sometimes referred to as the infinite tower of SDEs.

In his paper "The ''S''-Matrix in Quantum electrodynamics",<ref name="Dyson49">{{cite journal |author=F. Dyson |year=1949 |title=The ''S'' Matrix in Quantum Electrodynamics |journal=Phys. Rev. |volume=75 |issue=11 |page=1736 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.75.1736|bibcode = 1949PhRv...75.1736D }}</ref> Dyson derived relations between different [[S-matrix]] elements, or more specific "one-particle Green's functions", in [[quantum electrodynamics]], by summing up infinitely many [[Feynman diagram]]s, thus working in a perturbative approach. Starting from his [[Schwinger's quantum action principle|variational principle]], Schwinger derived a set of equations for Green's functions non-perturbatively,<ref name="Schwinger51">{{cite journal |author=J. Schwinger |year=1951 |title=On Green's functions of quantized fields I + II |journal=PNAS |volume=37 |issue=7 |pages=452–459 |bibcode = 1951PNAS...37..452S |doi = 10.1073/pnas.37.7.452 |pmc=1063400 |pmid=16578383|doi-access=free }}</ref> which generalize Dyson's equations to the Schwinger–Dyson equations for the Green functions of [[Quantum field theory|quantum field theories]]. Today they provide a non-perturbative approach to quantum field theories and applications can be found in many fields of [[theoretical physics]], such as [[solid-state physics]] and [[elementary particle physics]].

Schwinger also derived an equation for the two-particle irreducible Green functions,<ref name="Schwinger51"/> which is nowadays referred to as the inhomogeneous [[Bethe–Salpeter equation]].

== Derivation ==
Given a polynomially bounded [[functional (mathematics)|functional]] <math>F</math> over the field configurations, then, for any [[quantum state|state vector]] (which is a solution of the QFT), <math>|\psi\rangle</math>, we have

:<math>\left\langle\psi\left|\mathcal{T}\left\{\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi}F[\varphi]\right\}\right|\psi\right\rangle = -i\left\langle\psi\left|\mathcal{T}\left\{F[\varphi]\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi}S[\varphi]\right\}\right|\psi\right\rangle</math>

where <math display="inline">\frac{\delta}{\delta \varphi}</math> is the [[functional derivative]] with respect to <math>\varphi</math>, <math>S</math> is the [[action (physics)|action]] functional and <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is the [[time ordering]] operation.

Equivalently, in the [[density state]] formulation, for any (valid) density state <math>\rho</math>, we have

:<math>\rho\left(\mathcal{T}\left\{\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi}F[\varphi]\right\}\right) = -i\rho\left(\mathcal{T}\left\{ F[\varphi] \frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi}S[\varphi]\right\}\right).</math>

This [[infinite set]] of equations can be used to solve for the correlation functions [[nonperturbative]]ly.

To make the connection to diagrammatic techniques (like [[Feynman diagram]]s) clearer, it is often convenient to split the action <math>S</math> as

:<math>S[\varphi] = \tfrac{1}{2}\varphi^{i}D^{-1}_{ij}\varphi^{j} + S_{\text{int}}[\varphi],</math>

where the first term is the quadratic part and <math>D^{-1}</math> is an invertible symmetric (antisymmetric for fermions) covariant tensor of rank two in the [[deWitt notation]] whose inverse, <math>D</math> is called the bare propagator and <math>S_{\text{int}}[\varphi]</math> is the "interaction action". Then, we can rewrite the SD equations as

:<math>\left\langle\psi\left\vert\mathcal{T}\left\{F \varphi^j\right\}\right\vert\psi\right\rangle=\left\langle\psi\left\vert\mathcal{T}\left\{iF_{,i}D^{ij}-FS_{\text{int},i}D^{ij}\right\}\right\vert\psi\right\rangle.</math>

If <math>F</math> is a functional of <math>\varphi</math>, then for an [[Operator (physics)|operator]] <math>K</math>, <math>F[K]</math> is defined to be the operator which substitutes <math>K</math> for <math>\varphi</math>. For example, if

:<math>F[\varphi]=\frac{\partial^{k_1}}{\partial x_1^{k_1}}\varphi(x_1)\cdots \frac{\partial^{k_n}}{\partial x_n^{k_n}}\varphi(x_n)</math>

and <math>G</math> is a functional of <math>J</math>, then

:<math>F\left[-i\frac{\delta}{\delta J}\right]G[J]=(-i)^n \frac{\partial^{k_1}}{\partial x_1^{k_1}}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_1)} \cdots \frac{\partial^{k_n}}{\partial x_n^{k_n}}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_n)} G[J].</math>

If we have an "[[analytic function|analytic]]" (a function that is locally given by a convergent power series) [[functional (mathematics)|functional]] <math>Z</math> (called the [[generating functional]]) of <math>J</math> (called the [[source field]]) satisfying

:<math>\frac{\delta^n Z}{\delta J(x_1) \cdots \delta J(x_n)}[0]=i^n Z[0] \langle\varphi(x_1)\cdots \varphi(x_n)\rangle,</math>

then, from the properties of the functional integrals

:<math>{\left \langle \frac{\delta \mathcal{S}}{\delta \varphi(x)}\left[\varphi \right] + J(x)\right\rangle}_J=0,</math>

the Schwinger–Dyson equation for the generating functional is

:<math>\frac{\delta S}{\delta \varphi(x)}\left[-i \frac{\delta}{\delta J} \right] Z[J] + J(x)Z[J]=0.</math>

If we expand this equation as a [[Taylor series]] about <math>J = 0</math>, we get the entire set of Schwinger–Dyson equations.

==An example: ''φ''<sup>4</sup>==
To give an example, suppose

:<math>S[\varphi]=\int d^dx \left (\tfrac{1}{2} \partial^\mu \varphi(x) \partial_\mu \varphi(x) -\tfrac{1}{2}m^2\varphi(x)^2 -\frac{\lambda}{4!}\varphi(x)^4\right )</math>

for a real field&nbsp;<math> \varphi </math>.

Then,

:<math>\frac{\delta S}{\delta \varphi(x)}=-\partial_\mu \partial^\mu \varphi(x) -m^2 \varphi(x) - \frac{\lambda}{3!}\varphi^3(x).</math>

The Schwinger–Dyson equation for this particular example is:

:<math>i\partial_\mu \partial^\mu \frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}Z[J]+im^2\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}Z[J]-\frac{i\lambda}{3!}\frac{\delta^3}{\delta J(x)^3} Z[J] + J(x)Z[J] = 0</math>

Note that since

:<math>\frac{\delta^3}{\delta J(x)^3}</math>

is not well-defined because

:<math>\frac{\delta^3}{\delta J(x_1)\delta J(x_2) \delta J(x_3)} Z[J]</math>

is a [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]] in

:<math>x_1</math>, <math>x_2</math> and <math>x_3</math>,

this equation needs to be [[regularization (physics)|regularized]].

In this example, the bare propagator D is the [[Green's function]] for <math>-\partial^\mu \partial_\mu-m^2</math> and so, the Schwinger–Dyson set of equations goes as

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{ \varphi(x_0) \varphi(x_1)\} \mid \psi\rangle \\[4pt]
= {} & iD(x_0,x_1) +\frac{\lambda}{3!}\int d^dx_2 \, D(x_0,x_2) \langle \psi \mid \mathcal{T} \{\varphi(x_1)\varphi(x_2)\varphi(x_2)\varphi(x_2)\} \mid \psi\rangle
\end{align}
</math>

and

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{\varphi(x_0) \varphi(x_1) \varphi(x_2) \varphi(x_3)\} \mid \psi\rangle \\[6pt]
= {} & iD(x_0,x_1)\langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{\varphi(x_2)\varphi(x_3)\}\mid\psi\rangle + iD(x_0,x_2)\langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{\varphi(x_1)\varphi(x_3)\}\mid\psi\rangle \\[4pt]
& {} + iD(x_0,x_3)\langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{\varphi(x_1)\varphi(x_2)\}\mid\psi\rangle \\[4pt]
& {} + \frac{\lambda}{3!}\int d^dx_4 \, D(x_0,x_4)\langle\psi\mid\mathcal{T}\{\varphi(x_1)\varphi(x_2)\varphi(x_3)\varphi(x_4)\varphi(x_4)\varphi(x_4)\}\mid\psi\rangle
\end{align}
</math>

etc.

(Unless there is [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]], the odd correlation functions vanish.)
